content.title: Recommendations for the regimen and the duration of anticoagulation after pulmonary embolism in patients with active cancer (Section 8.6)
content.summary: Guidance on anticoagulation in patients with cancer who develop pulmonary embolism (PE). Emphasizes starting anticoagulation as soon as safe, no evidence to support routine use of venous filters as adjunct to anticoagulation in cancer patients, and management of incidental PE similar to symptomatic PE when certain anatomic criteria are met.
key_points: Do not delay the initiation of anticoagulation as soon as it is safe to do so.
There is no evidence to support the use of venous filters as an adjunct to anticoagulation treatment in patients with cancer.

Some patients presenting with PE without identifiable risk factors are diagnosed with cancer within the first year; however, comprehensive CT abdomen or 18F-FDG PET did not detect more cancers than limited screening in randomized trials.
Search for occult cancer after an episode of VTE may be limited to careful history, physical examination, basic laboratory tests, and chest X-ray (if no CTPA was performed to diagnose PE).

Incidental PE in patients with cancer should be managed the same as symptomatic PE when it involves segmental or more proximal branches, multiple subsegmental vessels, or a single subsegmental vessel in association with detectable DVT.

recommendations.recommendation: For patients with PE and cancer, weight-adjusted subcutaneous low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) should be considered for the first 6 months over vitamin K antagonists (VKAs).
Edoxaban may be considered as an alternative to weight-adjusted subcutaneous LMWH in patients without gastrointestinal cancer.
Rivaroxaban may be considered as an alternative to weight-adjusted subcutaneous LMWH in patients without gastrointestinal cancer.
For patients with PE and cancer, extended anticoagulation beyond the first 6 months should be considered for an indefinite period or until the cancer is cured.

Management of incidental PE should follow the same approach as symptomatic PE if it involves segmental or more proximal branches, multiple subsegmental vessels, or a single subsegmental vessel with proven DVT.

content.diagnostic_testing_notes: Two large randomized trials failed to show that comprehensive CT abdomen or 18F-FDG PET detected more cancers than limited screening in unprovoked VTE; thus extensive imaging for occult cancer is not routinely recommended beyond targeted evaluation.

abbreviations.18F-FDG: fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography using fluorine-18
